- **Synovial fluid WBC** in acute crystal arthritis is inflammatory (**about 2,000-50,000/mm3**, can exceed 50,000 and mimic sepsis).
- **Crystals and infection can coexist:** always send fluid for **Gram stain and culture**; finding crystals does not exclude septic arthritis.

## 2. Gout
### Epidemiology and pathophysiology
- Commonest inflammatory arthritis in men; prevalence about 1-4%; **men over 40**, women after menopause (oestrogen is uricosuric).
- **Hyperuricaemia:** serum urate **above 6.8 mg/dL (about 405 micromol/L)**, the saturation point for MSU at body temperature and pH. Most hyperuricaemic people never get gout.
- Humans lack **uricase**; urate is the end product of purine metabolism (xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine to uric acid).
- **Inflammation:** MSU crystals are phagocytosed by macrophages, activating the **NLRP3 inflammasome**, releasing **IL-1 beta**, and causing neutrophil influx (hence IL-1 blockers and colchicine work).
- Crystals form preferentially in **cooler, peripheral joints** and in damaged cartilage (first MTP).

### Causes of hyperuricaemia
| Mechanism | Causes |
|---|---|
| **Under-excretion (about 90%)** | **CKD**, **diuretics (thiazide, loop)**, **low-dose aspirin**, **ciclosporin, tacrolimus**, **pyrazinamide, ethambutol**, alcohol (lactate competes), lead (saturnine gout), dehydration, ketosis, hypothyroidism, metabolic syndrome, obesity, hypertension |
| **Over-production (about 10%)** | **Myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders, tumour lysis**, psoriasis, haemolysis, high purine diet, fructose, **Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (HGPRT deficiency)**, **PRPP synthetase overactivity**, glycogen storage disease type I |

### Clinical stages
1. **Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia** (not treated with drugs generally).
2. **Acute gout flare:** sudden, very painful, red, hot, swollen joint, maximal within **24 hours**, often at night; **first MTP joint (podagra) in about 50% of first attacks and about 90% eventually**; then midfoot, ankle, knee, wrist, olecranon bursa. Triggers: alcohol (especially beer), purine-rich food, dehydration, surgery, trauma, starting diuretics or **starting/changing urate-lowering therapy**. Settles in 1-2 weeks even untreated; overlying skin may desquamate.
3. **Intercritical gout:** asymptomatic intervals between attacks (crystals still present in joints).
4. **Chronic tophaceous gout:** after years of uncontrolled hyperuricaemia: **tophi** (helix of ear, olecranon bursa, Achilles, finger pads, extensor surfaces), chronic polyarthritis, joint destruction.
- **Systemic associations:** **urate nephrolithiasis**, chronic urate nephropathy, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, metabolic syndrome.
- **Tophi** may discharge chalky white material, ulcerate, become infected, compress nerves (**carpal tunnel syndrome**, cubital tunnel) or cause **tendon rupture**; tophus can mimic tumour or infection (spinal tophus causing cord compression is rare).

### Investigations
- **Joint aspiration: negatively birefringent needle crystals** (diagnostic, also between attacks in previously affected joints and from tophi).
- **Serum urate:** may be **normal during an acute flare** (in about a third; urate falls with inflammation); measure **2-4 weeks after** the flare for baseline and treatment target.
- Renal function, glucose, lipids, blood count (secondary causes, comorbidity).
- **Radiographs:** normal early.
  - Chronic: **"punched-out" juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges (Martel sign, "rat-bite")**.
  - **Joint space preserved until late**; **no periarticular osteopenia** (differs from RA).
  - Asymmetric soft-tissue swelling (tophi), which may calcify.
- **Ultrasound:** **double contour sign** (urate coating cartilage surface), tophi, "snowstorm" effusion.
- **Dual-energy CT (DECT):** colour-coded **urate deposits**; useful when aspiration is not possible.
- **ACR/EULAR 2015 classification criteria:** entry criterion = at least one episode of swelling, pain or tenderness of a peripheral joint or bursa; **sufficient criterion = MSU crystals in a symptomatic joint, bursa or tophus**; otherwise a weighted score (clinical pattern, urate level, imaging) with **8 or more** points classifying as gout.

### Treatment of acute flare
- Start **as early as possible** (within 24 hours), rest, ice, elevation.
- **First-line options (choose by comorbidity; ACR 2020, EULAR 2016):**
  - **NSAIDs** at full anti-inflammatory dose (e.g. naproxen); avoid in CKD, peptic ulcer, heart failure, anticoagulation.
  - **Low-dose colchicine:** **1.2 mg then 0.6 mg one hour later** (AGREE trial: as effective as high-dose with far less diarrhoea); then 0.5-0.6 mg once or twice daily. Reduce dose in renal impairment; **toxic interactions with CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein inhibitors** (clarithromycin, ciclosporin, ketoconazole, verapamil); side effects diarrhoea, myopathy, marrow suppression. **IV colchicine is not used.**
  - **Glucocorticoids:** oral prednisolone (about 30-35 mg/day for 3-5 days), **intra-articular injection** for a single large joint (after excluding infection), IM.
- **IL-1 inhibitors** (anakinra, canakinumab) for patients who cannot take the above.
- **Do not stop urate-lowering therapy** during a flare; ACR 2020 conditionally allows **starting ULT during a flare** (with anti-inflammatory cover).

### Urate-lowering therapy (ULT)
#### Indications (ACR 2020)
| Strength | Indications |
|---|---|
| **Strongly recommended** | **One or more subcutaneous tophi**, **radiographic damage due to gout**, **two or more flares per year** |
| Conditionally recommended | More than one previous flare but fewer than two per year; first flare with **CKD stage 3 or worse, serum urate over 9 mg/dL, or urolithiasis** |
| Generally not recommended | Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia |

- EULAR 2016: consider ULT from the first diagnosis, especially in young patients (under 40), very high urate (over 8 mg/dL), or comorbidities.

#### Targets and strategy
- **Treat-to-target: serum urate under 6 mg/dL (360 micromol/L)**; **under 5 mg/dL (300 micromol/L)** in severe/tophaceous gout (EULAR) until tophi dissolve. Lifelong in most patients.
- **Start low, go slow:** start allopurinol at **100 mg/day or less (50 mg in CKD stage 3 or worse)** and titrate every 2-5 weeks (up to 800-900 mg/day) to target, regardless of renal function (with monitoring).
- **Flare prophylaxis when starting ULT:** low-dose colchicine (0.5-0.6 mg once or twice daily), or low-dose NSAID or prednisolone, for **3-6 months** (mobilisation of crystals precipitates flares).

#### ULT drugs
| Drug | Mechanism | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| **Allopurinol** | **Xanthine oxidase inhibitor** (purine analogue) | **First-line** (including in CKD). **Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome / SJS-TEN / DRESS** (rare, often fatal): risk with **HLA-B5801**; **screen before starting in Han Chinese, Korean, Thai and African-American patients**; risk also with high starting dose and CKD. **Interaction: azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine** (toxicity; reduce dose drastically) |
| **Febuxostat** | Non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor | Second-line. **CARES trial: higher cardiovascular and all-cause death than allopurinol** in patients with CV disease (FDA boxed warning); **FAST trial did not confirm the excess risk**. Avoid where possible in established CV disease |
| **Probenecid** | **Uricosuric** (inhibits URAT1 reabsorption) | Avoid with urolithiasis, CKD (ineffective when eGFR low), urate over-producers; interacts with penicillin and methotrexate |
| Benzbromarone | Potent uricosuric | Hepatotoxicity; limited availability |
| Lesinurad | URAT1 inhibitor, used with XO inhibitor | Withdrawn commercially |
| **Pegloticase** | **Recombinant uricase** (IV every 2 weeks) | **Refractory tophaceous gout**; **check G6PD (haemolysis, methaemoglobinaemia)**; infusion reactions and antibodies (co-prescribe methotrexate) |
| Adjuncts | **Losartan** (mild uricosuric), **fenofibrate**, SGLT2 inhibitors | Useful for comorbidities; swap thiazide or loop diuretic if possible |

#### Lifestyle
- Weight loss, limit **alcohol (especially beer and spirits)**, **purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meat, shellfish)** and **fructose/high-fructose corn syrup** drinks.
- Low-fat dairy and coffee are associated with lower urate; vitamin C has a weak effect. Hydration.

### Surgical management of gout (orthopaedic role)
- **Indications for surgery:**
  - **Infected or ulcerated tophi**, chronic draining sinus
  - **Nerve compression** (carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel), **tendon rupture or triggering**, mechanical block
  - **Joint destruction:** **first MTP arthrodesis**, arthroplasty of knee or hip, wrist fusion
  - Cosmetic or functional problems from large tophi; **diagnostic biopsy** when tophus mimics tumour
- **Technique:** debulking/curettage of tophus (chalky material), careful skin handling (skin over tophi is thin; wound healing problems and sinus formation common), **perioperative flare risk** (continue ULT and prophylaxis).
- **Postoperative gout flare** is common in patients with gout (surgery, dehydration, fasting): differentiate from infection (aspirate).
- **Gout in a prosthetic joint** can mimic periprosthetic joint infection: aspirate and culture; crystals do not exclude infection.

## 3. Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD)
### Epidemiology and pathogenesis
- Disease of the **elderly** (prevalence of chondrocalcinosis rises sharply over 60; about half of people over 85).
- Excess **extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate** in cartilage (overproduction by chondrocytes, **ANKH** transporter mutations in familial cases) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals in **hyaline and fibrocartilage**.
- **Chondrocalcinosis** = radiographic calcification of cartilage; usually CPP, but not all chondrocalcinosis is symptomatic.

### Associations (screen if onset under 60 years or polyarticular/florid)
- **"4 H's" (main metabolic associations):**
  - **Haemochromatosis** (also hook-like osteophytes at 2nd and 3rd MCP joints)
  - **Hyperparathyroidism** (primary)
  - **Hypomagnesaemia** (including **Gitelman syndrome**)
  - **Hypophosphatasia** (low ALP)
- Others: **osteoarthritis**, previous joint trauma or meniscectomy, ageing, familial CPPD (ANKH), possibly hypothyroidism, gout, Wilson disease, acromegaly.
- **Screening tests:** serum calcium, magnesium, phosphate, ALP, ferritin and transferrin saturation, TSH.

### Clinical presentations (EULAR 2011 terminology)
| Presentation | Features |
|---|---|
| **Asymptomatic CPPD** | Incidental chondrocalcinosis on radiographs |
| **Acute CPP crystal arthritis ("pseudogout")** | Acute monoarthritis, **knee commonest**, then **wrist**, shoulder, ankle; elderly; can be triggered by **surgery (especially parathyroidectomy), intercurrent illness, trauma, IV fluids, bisphosphonates**; fever and raised CRP mimic sepsis |
| **OA with CPPD ("pseudo-OA")** | Commonest symptomatic form; **degenerative changes in atypical joints**: **radiocarpal (wrist)**, **isolated patellofemoral**, glenohumeral, elbow, MCP; prominent osteophytes and cysts |
| **Chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis ("pseudo-RA")** | Polyarticular, symmetric, morning stiffness, raised ESR: mimics rheumatoid arthritis |
| Pseudo-neuropathic (destructive) arthropathy | Severe destruction mimicking Charcot joint |
| **Crowned dens syndrome** | Acute neck pain, stiffness, fever in elderly; **CT shows calcification around the dens (transverse ligament)**; mimics meningitis or polymyalgia |
| Spinal CPPD | Ligamentum flavum calcification causing stenosis, discs |

- **SLAC wrist** (scapholunate advanced collapse) and **STT arthritis** are associated with CPPD (scapholunate ligament degeneration).

### Investigations
- **Synovial fluid:** **weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals** (gold standard); culture always.
- **Radiographs:** **chondrocalcinosis**: linear calcification in **menisci of the knee** (fibrocartilage) and hyaline cartilage, **triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) of the wrist**, **symphysis pubis**, acetabular labrum, intervertebral discs. Degenerative changes in atypical joints, large subchondral cysts.
- **Ultrasound:** hyperechoic deposits **within** the cartilage layer (vs urate on the **surface**: double contour sign).
- CT for crowned dens.

### Treatment
- **No therapy dissolves CPP crystals** (unlike urate-lowering therapy for gout).
- **Acute attack:** **joint aspiration** (relieves pain) **+ intra-articular corticosteroid** (once infection excluded), ice, rest; NSAIDs or **low-dose colchicine**; oral/IM steroids or IL-1 blockade (anakinra) for polyarticular or resistant cases.
- **Prophylaxis** of frequent attacks: low-dose colchicine or NSAID.
- **Chronic inflammatory CPP arthritis:** NSAIDs, colchicine, low-dose steroids, **hydroxychloroquine or methotrexate** (limited evidence).
- **Treat the underlying cause** (e.g. venesection in haemochromatosis, correct magnesium, parathyroidectomy) though established deposits may not regress.
- **Surgery:** as for OA: arthroplasty outcomes are similar to OA; wrist fusion or proximal row carpectomy for SLAC; decompression for spinal stenosis.

## 4. Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) deposition
### Calcific tendinitis (calcifying tendinopathy)
- **Supraspinatus** commonest (about 1-1.5 cm from insertion, the critical zone), then infraspinatus; also hip abductors (gluteus medius), longus colli (retropharyngeal tendinitis), wrist (FCU), elbow.
- **Women aged 30-60**; associated with diabetes and thyroid disease; **not degenerative** and **not associated with full-thickness cuff tears** (cell-mediated, reactive calcification).
- **Uhthoff stages:**
  1. **Precalcific (formative):** fibrocartilaginous metaplasia of tenocytes.
  2. **Calcific:** formative phase (chalk-like dense deposit, relatively painless), resting phase, then **resorptive phase** (toothpaste-like, macrophage and vascular invasion, **most painful**, deposit becomes fluffy and ill-defined; may rupture into subacromial bursa causing acute severe pain).
  3. **Postcalcific:** tendon remodels, healing.
- **Gartner radiographic classification:** type I dense, well-circumscribed (formative); type II mixed; type III translucent, cloudy, poorly defined (resorptive; likely to resolve spontaneously).
- **Treatment:**
  - **Conservative first** (most resolve): NSAIDs, physiotherapy, subacromial steroid injection.
  - **Ultrasound-guided needle lavage (barbotage)** of the deposit: good evidence for pain relief.
  - **Extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT)**, high energy, for type I/II deposits.
  - **Arthroscopic removal** (with or without subacromial decompression) for persistent symptoms after about 6 months of failed conservative care; repair tendon if large defect.

### Milwaukee shoulder syndrome
- **Elderly women**, destructive arthropathy of the **glenohumeral joint** with **massive rotator cuff tear**, large (often **blood-stained**) effusion with **BCP crystals** (alizarin red positive) and low WBC count.
- Radiographs: superior humeral head migration, destruction of humeral head and glenoid (similar to cuff tear arthropathy).
- Treatment: aspiration, steroid injection, NSAIDs, physiotherapy; **reverse total shoulder arthroplasty** for severe cases.

## 5. Differential diagnosis of an acute hot joint
| Condition | Clues |
|---|---|
| **Septic arthritis** | Must be excluded first: fever, rigors, high WBC; **culture positive**; crystals can coexist |
| **Gout** | Middle-aged man, first MTP, diuretics/alcohol, tophi, needle-shaped negative crystals |
| **Pseudogout (CPPD)** | Elderly, knee or wrist, chondrocalcinosis, rhomboid positive crystals |
| Cellulitis or bursitis | Skin infection without joint effusion; prepatellar or olecranon bursitis (gout or infection) |
| Reactive arthritis | After GI/GU infection, oligoarthritis lower limb, conjunctivitis, urethritis, enthesitis |
| Psoriatic arthritis | Dactylitis, DIP joints, nail pitting, pencil-in-cup |
| Rheumatoid arthritis | Symmetric small joints, periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, RF/anti-CCP |
| Trauma / haemarthrosis | History of injury, anticoagulants, haemophilia |

### Radiological distinction: gout vs RA vs CPPD
| Feature | Gout | Rheumatoid arthritis | CPPD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Erosions | **Punched-out, sclerotic margins, overhanging edges**, juxta-articular | **Marginal ("bare area")**, no sclerosis | Large subchondral cysts |
| Joint space | **Preserved until late** | Symmetric narrowing early | Narrowed (OA-like) |
| Bone density | **Normal** | **Periarticular osteopenia** | Normal |
| Distribution | Asymmetric; first MTP | Symmetric MCP, PIP, wrist | Knee, wrist (radiocarpal), PFJ |
| Soft tissue | Tophi (may calcify) | Fusiform swelling | **Chondrocalcinosis** |

## 6. Key "most common" facts
- **Commonest site of gout:** first MTP joint. **Commonest site of pseudogout:** knee. **Commonest site of chondrocalcinosis:** knee menisci (then TFCC, symphysis pubis).
- **Commonest cause of hyperuricaemia:** reduced renal excretion.
- **Commonest site of calcific tendinitis:** supraspinatus.
- **Serum urate can be normal in an acute attack.**
- **Allopurinol is first-line ULT, including in CKD** (low starting dose, titrate).
- **Colchicine** works by inhibiting **microtubule polymerisation** (tubulin binding), reducing neutrophil migration and NLRP3 activation.

> Exam pearl: **Gout = needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent (yellow parallel). CPPD = rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent (blue parallel). BCP = not birefringent, alizarin red.** Always culture: crystals and sepsis coexist.

> Exam pearl: **Gout radiograph:** punched-out erosions with sclerotic overhanging edges, preserved joint space, no osteopenia. **ULT** if tophi, radiographic damage or 2 or more flares/year; target urate under 6 mg/dL (under 5 with tophi); start allopurinol low with colchicine prophylaxis; HLA-B5801 screening in at-risk ethnic groups. **CARES:** febuxostat higher CV death.

> Exam pearl: **CPPD associations = 4 H's** (haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphatasia): screen if under 60. OA in atypical joints (radiocarpal, isolated PFJ, glenohumeral) suggests CPPD; **crowned dens syndrome** = neck pain + fever + dens calcification on CT. **Calcific tendinitis resorptive phase is the most painful.**

Paget and metabolic bone.md:
# Part A: Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans)

## 1. Definition and epidemiology
- A **localised disorder of bone remodelling**: excessive, disorganised **osteoclastic resorption** followed by compensatory, chaotic **osteoblastic formation**, giving bone that is **enlarged, vascular, weak and deformed**.
- **Second commonest metabolic bone disease** after osteoporosis.
- **Age:** rare before 40; prevalence rises with age (about 2-4% of people over 55 in high-prevalence countries). Slight **male predominance**.
- **Geography:** commonest in the **UK** (highest in Lancashire), western Europe, and their emigrants (Australia, New Zealand, North America). **Rare in Asia (including India), Africa and Scandinavia.** Prevalence and severity have **declined** over recent decades.
- **Polyostotic in about two-thirds**, monostotic in about one-third. **New sites rarely appear after diagnosis**; disease spreads within an affected bone, not to new bones.

## 2. Aetiology and pathology
- **Genetic:** **SQSTM1** (sequestosome-1, **p62**, a protein in the RANK/NF-kappa-B pathway of osteoclasts) mutations in about **40% of familial** and **5-10% of sporadic** cases; autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance. Other loci: TNFRSF11A (RANK) in familial expansile osteolysis-like syndromes, OPTN, CSF1.
- **Environmental (debated):** **paramyxovirus** hypothesis (measles, RSV, canine distemper): **nucleocapsid-like inclusions in osteoclast nuclei** on electron microscopy. Not proven.
- **Osteoclasts** are **increased in number and size** (up to **100 nuclei**, normal up to about 10) and hyper-responsive to RANKL and vitamin D.
- **Three phases** (may coexist in one patient):

| Phase | Pathology | Radiograph |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Lytic (osteolytic, "hot")** | Intense osteoclastic resorption, fibrovascular marrow | Advancing **"blade of grass" / "flame-shaped"** lytic front in long bones; **osteoporosis circumscripta** in the skull |
| **2. Mixed** | Resorption and chaotic formation | Coarse trabeculae, cortical thickening, bone enlargement |
| **3. Sclerotic ("burnt-out")** | Reduced cellularity, dense bone | Sclerosis, enlargement, deformity |

- **Histology:** **mosaic pattern** of lamellar bone with irregular **cement (reversal) lines** (jigsaw pattern), woven bone, fibrovascular marrow, giant osteoclasts.
- Pagetic bone is **larger but mechanically weaker** (poor architecture) and **hypervascular** (arteriovenous shunting).

## 3. Sites
- **Pelvis (commonest)**, then lumbar spine, femur, skull, tibia, sacrum, humerus. Hands and feet are rarely affected.
- In long bones, disease **starts at one end (subchondral bone) and advances along the shaft** (the tibia is an exception where it may start in the diaphysis/tuberosity region).

## 4. Clinical features
- **Most are asymptomatic**: found because of a **raised ALP** or an incidental radiograph.
- **Bone pain:** deep, aching, constant, **worse at rest and at night**; may be due to the disease itself (responds to bisphosphonates), to **secondary OA**, to fissure fractures, or to **sarcoma** (new, severe, progressive pain).
- **Deformity:** **anterolateral bowing of the femur**, **anterior bowing of the tibia** (sabre tibia), kyphosis, **skull enlargement** (increasing hat size, frontal bossing), **coxa vara**.
- **Warmth** over affected bone (increased vascularity).
- **Joint involvement:** **secondary osteoarthritis** of the hip (with **protrusio acetabuli**) and knee (varus).
- **Neurological:**
  - **Deafness** (commonest neurological complication; cochlear and ossicular involvement; conductive and sensorineural).
  - Cranial nerve palsies, **basilar invagination** (hydrocephalus, brainstem compression).
  - **Spinal stenosis** and cord compression (vertebral enlargement, epidural vascular steal); often **responds to bisphosphonates** before surgery is needed.
- **Fractures:**
  - **Fissure (incomplete, stress) fractures on the convex (tension) side** of a bowed femur or tibia; painful; may progress to complete fracture.
  - **Complete "banana" fractures:** **transverse**, typically **subtrochanteric** femur; high rate of **delayed union/non-union** (especially femoral neck).
- **Metabolic and systemic:** **high-output cardiac failure** (rare, extensive disease), **hypercalcaemia when immobilised** (e.g. after fracture), hypercalciuria and stones, aortic stenosis/calcification.
- **Neoplasia:**
  - **Paget sarcoma** in about **1% or less** (higher with extensive polyostotic disease): **osteosarcoma** commonest, also fibrosarcoma, MFH/UPS, chondrosarcoma. Sites: **pelvis, femur, humerus**, skull. Presents with **new pain, swelling, pathological fracture**, lytic destruction and soft-tissue mass. **Very poor prognosis** (5-year survival under about 10%). Paget accounts for a large share of **osteosarcoma in patients over 60** (the second peak).
  - **Giant cell tumour** in pagetic bone (skull, facial bones), often multifocal, may respond to steroids.

## 5. Investigations
### Biochemistry
| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| **Serum ALP (total / bone-specific)** | **Raised**; best routine marker of **activity and extent**; used to monitor treatment |
| Serum calcium and phosphate | **Normal** (calcium rises with **immobilisation**) |
| PTH | Normal (may be raised if vitamin D deficient or after bisphosphonate) |
| Resorption markers (urinary hydroxyproline, NTX, serum CTX) | Raised |
| Formation marker P1NP | Raised; useful when monostotic disease or liver disease makes ALP unreliable |

- **Normal ALP does not exclude** Paget (limited monostotic disease). Check **liver function** (GGT) to confirm bone origin of ALP.
- Check **25(OH) vitamin D** before bisphosphonates.

### Imaging
- **Plain radiographs** (diagnostic): **enlargement of bone**, **cortical thickening**, **coarse trabeculae**, mixed lysis and sclerosis, bowing.
- **Classic signs:**
  - **Skull:** **osteoporosis circumscripta** (lytic phase, frontal/occipital), **"cotton wool" skull** (mixed), diploic widening, "Tam o'Shanter" skull, basilar invagination.
  - **Vertebra:** **"picture frame" vertebra** (thick peripheral cortex, enlarged body), **"ivory" vertebra** (dense, enlarged).
  - **Pelvis:** **thickened iliopectineal line ("brim sign")**, **protrusio acetabuli**, enlarged pubic rami and ischium.
  - **Long bones:** **"blade of grass" / "candle flame"** lytic front, bowing, fissure fractures on the convex cortex.
- **Isotope bone scan:** **intense uptake**; best to **map the extent** of polyostotic disease at diagnosis (recommended by guidelines).
- **CT / MRI:** for spinal stenosis, basilar invagination, and **suspected sarcoma** (cortical destruction, soft-tissue mass; **marrow fat is preserved in uncomplicated Paget on MRI**, lost in sarcoma).
- **Biopsy:** only if the diagnosis is uncertain or sarcoma or metastasis is suspected.

### Differential diagnosis of an enlarged, dense bone or ivory vertebra
| Condition | Distinguishing point |
|---|---|
| **Paget disease** | **Bone is enlarged**, cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae |
| **Osteoblastic metastasis (prostate, breast)** | **Bone not enlarged**, multiple discrete lesions, high PSA; pedicle involvement |
| **Lymphoma (Hodgkin)** | Ivory vertebra **without enlargement**; anterior scalloping |
| Fibrous dysplasia | Younger, ground-glass, shepherd's crook |
| Hyperparathyroidism / renal osteodystrophy | Subperiosteal resorption, rugger-jersey spine, abnormal calcium/PTH |
| Fluorosis | Diffuse sclerosis with ligament calcification, endemic area |

## 6. Medical management
### Who to treat
- **Bone pain attributable to active Paget disease** is the **main evidence-based indication** (Endocrine Society guideline 2014; international Paget guideline, Ralston et al. 2019).
- **Commonly recommended (weaker evidence, debated):** active disease at sites where complications are likely (**skull, spine, weight-bearing long bones, near major joints**), **before elective surgery** on pagetic bone, **hypercalcaemia of immobilisation**, young patients with active disease, neurological complications (spinal stenosis often improves).
- **PRISM trial (Langston et al. 2010):** **intensive** bisphosphonate treatment aiming to normalise ALP vs **symptomatic** treatment: **no difference** in fractures, orthopaedic surgery, hearing loss, pain or quality of life. Hence the 2019 guideline **does not recommend treating asymptomatic patients simply to normalise ALP** or prevent complications.
- **ZiPP trial (2024):** **prophylactic zoledronate in SQSTM1 mutation carriers** without established disease reduced the development of new lesions (a newer, still-evolving area).

### Drugs
| Drug | Regimen | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| **Zoledronic acid** | **5 mg IV single infusion** | **Drug of choice**: highest response rate and **longest remission** (superior to risedronate; **Reid et al. NEJM 2005**); remission often lasts years |
| Risedronate | 30 mg oral daily for 2 months | Alternative |
| Alendronate | 40 mg oral daily for 6 months | Alternative |
| Pamidronate | IV infusions | Alternative, more infusions |
| Etidronate | Oral | **Obsolete**: high doses impair mineralisation (osteomalacia) |
| **Calcitonin** | SC injection | Second-line (bisphosphonate intolerance); short-lived effect |
| Denosumab | | Not standard; rebound on stopping |

- **Correct vitamin D and calcium first**: zoledronate can cause **symptomatic hypocalcaemia**. Other effects: acute-phase reaction (flu-like), renal toxicity (avoid if creatinine clearance under 35 mL/min), osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare at these doses).
- **Monitoring:** ALP at 3-6 months then yearly; re-treat if pain recurs with a rise in ALP.
- Analgesics and NSAIDs for pain from secondary OA.

## 7. Surgical management
### General principles
- **Pre-treat with a bisphosphonate** (traditionally **6 weeks to 3 months** before elective surgery) to **reduce hypervascularity and blood loss** (widely taught; evidence is limited).
- Expect **heavy bleeding**, **hard sclerotic bone** (burr/reamers, high-speed tools, cooling), **deformity** (bowing makes straight nails difficult), **wide medullary canals**, **delayed union**, and **heterotopic ossification** after hip surgery.
- **Mobilise early**; watch for **hypercalcaemia of immobilisation**.

### Specific problems
- **Hip OA (protrusio, coxa vara):**
  - **THA** gives good pain relief. Problems: protrusio (medial wall reconstruction, bone graft, cups placed at the anatomical centre), femoral bowing (may need **corrective osteotomy**), hard bone, bleeding, **heterotopic ossification** (consider prophylaxis).
  - Both **cemented and uncemented** fixation give acceptable results; pain from active Paget may persist if untreated medically. Distinguish Paget pain from OA pain before arthroplasty.
- **Knee OA (varus):** **TKA** (deformity correction, hard bone; patellar involvement); **high tibial osteotomy** for younger patients with deformity.
- **Tibial / femoral bowing with fissure fractures:** **corrective osteotomy with intramedullary nail** (prophylactic stabilisation).
- **Fractures:**
  - **Femoral neck:** **high non-union rate with internal fixation**: prefer **arthroplasty** (hemi or total).
  - **Subtrochanteric / shaft ("banana") fractures:** **intramedullary (cephalomedullary) nailing**, often with **corrective osteotomy** to allow nail passage; plates are less favoured (high failure in weak, bowed bone). Union is often delayed.
  - **Pertrochanteric:** usual fixation; may need a long nail.
- **Spinal stenosis:** medical treatment first (often improves); **decompression** if failed or with progressive deficit (expect bleeding).
- **Paget sarcoma:** biopsy, staging, chemotherapy and wide resection/amputation; prognosis remains poor.

> Exam pearl: Paget = **enlarged** bone with **thick cortices and coarse trabeculae**, normal calcium and phosphate, **high ALP**. **Pelvis** commonest site. **Deafness** commonest neurological complication. **Zoledronate 5 mg single infusion** is the drug of choice. Sarcoma (**osteosarcoma**) under 1%, with **new pain** as the warning sign. Femoral neck fracture in Paget: **replace, do not fix**.

# Part B: Other metabolic bone disorders

## 8. Calcium-phosphate biochemistry master table

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Osteoporosis** | N | N | N | N | N | Quantity defect; normal mineralisation |
| **Paget disease** | N (high if immobile) | N | **High** | N | N | Bone enlargement |
| **Nutritional osteomalacia / rickets** | Low or N | **Low** | **High** | **High** | **Low** | Mineralisation defect |
| **Primary hyperparathyroidism** | **High** | **Low** | N or high | **High** | N | Adenoma |
| **Secondary HPT (CKD)** | Low or N | **High** | High | **High** | N or low | Renal osteodystrophy |

## 9. Hyperparathyroidism
### Primary hyperparathyroidism
- **Causes:** **single adenoma (about 85%)**, four-gland **hyperplasia** (about 15%; **MEN 1 and MEN 2A**), **carcinoma** (under 1%; very high calcium, palpable neck mass).
- **Commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in outpatients** (malignancy is commonest in hospital inpatients). Most are now **asymptomatic**, detected on routine calcium.
- **Clinical:** "**bones, stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans**"; fatigue, polyuria, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, hypertension.
- **Bone effects:**
  - **Cortical bone loss** more than trabecular (**distal radius / forearm** BMD falls most; spine relatively preserved).
  - **Osteitis fibrosa cystica** (severe, now rare): osteoclastic resorption with fibrous replacement of marrow and cysts.
  - **Brown tumours:** lytic, expansile lesions of **osteoclast-like giant cells, fibrous stroma and haemosiderin** (brown colour). Histologically similar to **giant cell tumour** and giant cell reparative granuloma: **always check calcium and PTH in a "giant cell lesion"** in an unusual site (jaw, pelvis, ribs, multiple). They **regress after parathyroidectomy**.
  - **Chondrocalcinosis** and pseudogout (CPPD).
- **Radiographs:**
  - **Subperiosteal resorption on the radial side of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers**: **pathognomonic**.
  - **Acro-osteolysis** (terminal tufts), **resorption of the distal clavicle**, medial tibia, symphysis pubis and sacroiliac joints.
  - **"Salt-and-pepper" (pepper-pot) skull**, **loss of the lamina dura** around teeth.
  - Brown tumours; **rugger-jersey spine** (more typical of secondary HPT).
- **Investigation:** high calcium with **inappropriately high (non-suppressed) PTH**; 24-hour urinary calcium (excludes **familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia**, a benign mimic with low urinary calcium); **sestamibi scan and neck ultrasound** to localise the adenoma.
- **Treatment:** **parathyroidectomy** (curative; increases BMD and reduces fracture risk). Indications in asymptomatic patients (international workshop criteria): serum calcium over 1 mg/dL (0.25 mmol/L) above the upper limit, **T-score -2.5 or below at any site or vertebral fracture**, renal stones/nephrocalcinosis or reduced creatinine clearance, hypercalciuria, **age under 50**. Medical: cinacalcet (calcimimetic), bisphosphonates.
- **Hungry bone syndrome** after parathyroidectomy: severe **hypocalcaemia** and hypophosphataemia as bone avidly remineralises.

### Secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism
- **Secondary:** appropriate PTH rise to **low calcium**: **chronic kidney disease**, **vitamin D deficiency**, malabsorption.
- **Tertiary:** long-standing secondary HPT becomes **autonomous** (often after renal transplant): **hypercalcaemia**; treated by parathyroidectomy.

## 10. Renal osteodystrophy (CKD-mineral and bone disorder, CKD-MBD)
- **Mechanism:** falling GFR causes **phosphate retention**, **raised FGF23**, **reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylase** activity (low 1,25(OH)2D), **low calcium**, and **secondary hyperparathyroidism**; metabolic acidosis adds to bone loss.
- **Types (by bone turnover, on biopsy):**

| Type | Turnover | Features |
|---|---|---|
| **Osteitis fibrosa (hyperparathyroid bone disease)** | **High** | Secondary HPT, subperiosteal resorption, brown tumours |
| **Adynamic bone disease** | **Low** | **Now the commonest form** (dialysis, diabetes, over-suppression of PTH by calcium/vitamin D); low PTH; fractures |
| **Osteomalacia** | Low | Historically **aluminium toxicity** (dialysate, phosphate binders) |
| **Mixed uraemic osteodystrophy** | Variable | Features of high turnover plus mineralisation defect |

- **Radiographs:** **rugger-jersey spine** (dense endplate bands with lucent middle), subperiosteal resorption, **soft-tissue and vascular calcification**, rickets-like changes in children (**renal rickets**; **slipped epiphyses**, genu valgum).
- **Orthopaedic problems:**
  - **Fragility fractures** (hip fracture risk several times normal; high mortality); poor fixation in soft bone.
  - **Spontaneous tendon ruptures** (**quadriceps**, patellar, triceps; often **bilateral**).
  - **Dialysis-related (beta-2 microglobulin) amyloidosis** after years of haemodialysis: **carpal tunnel syndrome** (often bilateral), **destructive spondyloarthropathy** (cervical), subchondral **bone cysts** (hip, carpus) that can cause pathological fracture, trigger finger.
  - **Calciphylaxis** (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy): painful skin necrosis.
  - **SCFE** in children with renal failure (often bilateral; treat the metabolic disease plus pinning).
  - **Higher infection and wound complications** after arthroplasty; avoid fistula arm for lines and tourniquets.
- **Medical:** phosphate restriction and **binders** (non-calcium binders: sevelamer, lanthanum), active vitamin D (calcitriol, alfacalcidol), **cinacalcet**, parathyroidectomy for refractory HPT.

## 11. Other metabolic and storage conditions examiners use
### Hypophosphatasia
- **ALPL gene** (tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase) mutation; **low serum ALP** is the hallmark.
- Accumulation of substrates: **raised urinary phosphoethanolamine** and **raised serum pyridoxal-5-phosphate** (vitamin B6); inorganic pyrophosphate inhibits mineralisation.
- **Perinatal/infantile** forms (rickets-like, craniosynostosis, seizures, often lethal); **childhood** form with **premature loss of deciduous teeth** (with roots intact); **adult** form with **metatarsal stress fractures**, femoral pseudofractures (**lateral subtrochanteric**, like atypical femoral fractures), chondrocalcinosis.
- **Treatment:** **asfotase alfa** (enzyme replacement). **Bisphosphonates are contraindicated** (they are pyrophosphate analogues and worsen mineralisation). Femoral pseudofractures: **intramedullary nail** (plates fail).

### Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency)
- **Defective hydroxylation of proline and lysine** in collagen synthesis: weak collagen, capillary fragility, **osteoid production fails** (osteoblast defect, not a mineralisation defect).
- **Clinical:** irritability and **pseudoparalysis** in infants (painful **subperiosteal haemorrhage**), gum bleeding (if teeth), perifollicular haemorrhage, **corkscrew hairs**, poor wound healing. Seen in restricted diets, alcoholism, autism with food selectivity, elderly.
- **Radiographs:**
  - **White line of Frankel** (dense zone of provisional calcification).
  - **Trummerfeld zone** (lucent band below it, the "scurvy line").
  - **Wimberger ring sign** (sclerotic rim around the epiphysis; do not confuse with the **Wimberger sign of congenital syphilis**, bilateral medial proximal tibial metaphyseal erosion).
  - **Pelkan spurs** (metaphyseal spurs), **corner (Park) fractures**, ground-glass osteopenia, calcifying subperiosteal haematomas during healing.
- **Physeal zone affected:** **metaphysis (primary spongiosa)**.
- **Treatment:** vitamin C; rapid response.

### Skeletal fluorosis (important in India)
- **Endemic** where drinking water fluoride exceeds about **1.5 mg/L** (parts of Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh/Telangana, Gujarat, Punjab, Karnataka); also from industrial exposure and some teas.
- **Fluoride replaces hydroxyl in hydroxyapatite (fluorapatite)**: dense but **brittle** bone.
- **Clinical:** **dental fluorosis** (mottled, brown-stained enamel; earliest sign in children), joint pain and stiffness, **spinal rigidity** (resembles ankylosing spondylitis), **compressive myelopathy and radiculopathy** (ossified ligamentum flavum/PLL, canal stenosis), **genu valgum** in children of endemic areas (with secondary hyperparathyroidism).
- **Radiographs:** **diffuse osteosclerosis** (spine, pelvis, ribs), **calcification of ligaments and interosseous membranes (forearm, leg)**, sacrotuberous/sacrospinous ligament ossification, periosteal new bone, osteophytes.
- **Management:** safe water (defluoridation), calcium, vitamin D; **decompression** (laminectomy) for myelopathy.

### Gaucher disease
- Commonest lysosomal storage disease; AR; **glucocerebrosidase** deficiency; **Ashkenazi Jews**; Gaucher cells (lipid-laden macrophages, "crumpled tissue paper").
- **Bone:** **Erlenmeyer flask distal femur**, osteopenia, **osteonecrosis** (femoral head, humeral head), **bone crises** (severe pain, fever, raised ESR that mimic **osteomyelitis**: treat with analgesia and do not drain, as surgery invites infection), pathological fractures, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia (bleeding at surgery).
- **Treatment:** enzyme replacement (imiglucerase) or substrate reduction (eliglustat).

### Pseudohypoparathyroidism and Albright hereditary osteodystrophy
- End-organ resistance to PTH (**GNAS** mutation): low calcium, high phosphate, **high PTH**.
- **Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype:** short stature, round face, obesity, **short fourth and fifth metacarpals** (and metatarsals), subcutaneous ossification, intellectual disability.
- **Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism:** same phenotype with **normal biochemistry** (paternal inheritance of the mutation).

### Other conditions with orthopaedic relevance
- **Hyperthyroidism:** increased bone turnover, osteoporosis; **thyroid acropachy** (periosteal new bone in the hands, digital clubbing) in Graves disease.
- **Hypothyroidism (cretinism):** delayed skeletal maturation, **epiphyseal dysgenesis** (fragmented femoral heads that mimic Perthes), **SCFE**.
- **Cushing syndrome / glucocorticoids:** commonest cause of **secondary osteoporosis**; vertebral fractures, **osteonecrosis**, decreased osteoblast function.
- **Acromegaly:** enlarged hands and feet, spade-like terminal tufts, **thick heel pad** (over about 22-25 mm), widened joint spaces then OA, carpal tunnel syndrome.
- **Heavy metals:** **lead lines** (dense metaphyseal bands in children; do not mistake for rickets or scurvy); **aluminium** (osteomalacia in dialysis).
- **Hypervitaminosis A:** cortical hyperostosis, premature physeal closure; **hypervitaminosis D:** hypercalcaemia, metastatic calcification.
- **Tumour-induced osteomalacia:** **phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour** secreting **FGF23**; low phosphate, bone pain, fractures; locate with **Ga-68 DOTATATE PET**; cure by excision (covered in the rickets note).

## 12. Osteoporosis: classification and secondary causes (drug treatment is in the osteoporosis drugs note)
- **Definition:** low bone mass with micro-architectural deterioration; **normal mineralisation** (quantity, not quality, of mineral).
- **Primary types:**

| Type | Who | Bone lost | Typical fractures |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Type I (postmenopausal)** | Women 50-70, oestrogen deficiency | Mainly **trabecular** | **Vertebral body, distal radius** |
| **Type II (senile)** | Men and women over 70 | **Trabecular and cortical** | **Hip**, pelvis, proximal humerus, vertebrae |

- **Secondary causes to screen for:** **glucocorticoids** (commonest), hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption (coeliac), alcohol, smoking, **rheumatoid arthritis**, CKD, myeloma (check serum protein electrophoresis), anticonvulsants, heparin, aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation, proton-pump inhibitors, immobilisation, diabetes (especially type 1).
- **Basic work-up:** calcium, phosphate, ALP, creatinine, 25(OH)D, PTH, TSH, full blood count, ESR/protein electrophoresis, testosterone in men, coeliac serology where indicated.
- **Peak bone mass** is reached in the **third decade**; loss accelerates for several years after **menopause**.

> Exam pearl: **Subperiosteal resorption on the radial side of the middle phalanges** = hyperparathyroidism. **Brown tumour** = check calcium/PTH before calling it a giant cell tumour. **Rugger-jersey spine** = renal osteodystrophy (also osteopetrosis). **Low ALP** = hypophosphatasia (avoid bisphosphonates). **Ligament and interosseous membrane calcification with sclerosis** = fluorosis.

osteonecrosis.md:
## 1. Definition and terminology
- **Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis, AVN, aseptic necrosis):** death of bone cells and marrow due to **interrupted blood supply**, followed by an attempt at repair that may end in **subchondral collapse** and **secondary arthritis**.
- **Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH)** is by far the commonest and most examined; then **humeral head**, knee (femoral condyles), talus, scaphoid, lunate.
- **Epidemiology of ONFH:** typically **30-50 years**, male predominance; accounts for about **5-12% of THAs** (higher proportion in Asia, including India). **Bilateral in about 50-80% of non-traumatic cases**: always image the **other hip** (MRI) at presentation.

## 2. Applied anatomy: blood supply of the femoral head
- **Medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA)**: **main supply** in adults, via the **lateral (superior) epiphyseal / posterosuperior retinacular arteries** that run under the synovium along the posterosuperior neck.
  - The deep branch of the MFCA passes **posterior to obturator externus** and **anterior to the short external rotators** (gemelli, obturator internus): basis of the **surgical dislocation (Ganz)** approach that preserves it, and of **repairing the short rotators** in the posterior approach.
- **Lateral femoral circumflex artery**: inferior metaphyseal and anterior neck supply (minor).
- **Artery of the ligamentum teres** (from obturator or MFCA): small contribution to the fovea; not enough alone.
- **Metaphyseal (intraosseous) vessels** cross the physis only after it closes.
- **Children:** between about **4 and 7 years** the femoral head depends almost entirely on the lateral epiphyseal vessels (basis of vulnerability in Perthes).

## 3. Aetiology
### Traumatic
- **Displaced femoral neck fracture** (AVN about **20-30%**; less after undisplaced fractures), **hip dislocation** (risk rises with **reduction delayed beyond about 6 hours**), femoral head fractures, **SCFE** (especially unstable), **talar neck fractures** (Hawkins), **scaphoid waist/proximal pole fractures**, 4-part proximal humerus fractures (Hertel criteria: metaphyseal head extension under 8 mm and disrupted medial hinge predict ischaemia).

### Non-traumatic (mnemonic-free list; know the commonest)
- **Corticosteroids**: **commonest non-traumatic cause**. Risk relates to **dose and duration** (high-dose pulses, transplant, SLE, leukaemia chemotherapy, **post-COVID-19 steroid use** reported especially from India). Inhaled and low-dose short courses carry little risk.
- **Alcohol** (second commonest; dose-dependent).
- **Haemoglobinopathies:** **sickle cell disease** (HbSS and HbSC), thalassaemia.
- **Coagulation disorders:** thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, antiphospholipid antibodies, raised lipoprotein(a)), hypofibrinolysis.
- **Dysbaric (Caisson disease)**: divers and tunnel workers; nitrogen bubbles; **juxta-articular** lesions (humeral head, femoral head, distal femur).
- **Gaucher disease**, SLE (steroid and vasculitis), HIV (and protease inhibitors), **radiation**, chemotherapy, **organ transplant** (renal), pancreatitis, hyperlipidaemia, pregnancy, smoking, hyperuricaemia/gout.
- **Idiopathic** in about 20-40%.

### ARCO 2019 criteria for steroid- and alcohol-associated ONFH
| Association | Criteria |
|---|---|
| **Glucocorticoid-associated** | **Over 2 g prednisolone (or equivalent) within a 3-month period**; ONFH diagnosed **within 2 years** of use; other risk factors excluded |
| **Alcohol-associated** | **Over 400 mL of pure ethanol per week (about 320 g) for more than 6 months**; ONFH diagnosed **within 1 year** of this intake; other risk factors excluded |

## 4. Pathophysiology
- **Final common pathway: ischaemia** of the subchondral bone. Mechanisms:
  - **Vascular interruption** (fracture, dislocation).
  - **Intravascular occlusion:** fat emboli, thrombosis (coagulopathy), sickled cells, nitrogen bubbles.
  - **Extravascular compression / raised intraosseous pressure:** marrow fat hypertrophy (steroids, alcohol), Gaucher cells; the femoral head behaves like a **closed compartment** (rationale for core decompression).
  - **Direct cell toxicity** (steroids impair osteoblast and osteocyte survival; radiation, chemotherapy).
- **Sequence:** cell death (osteocytes die within **12-48 hours** of ischaemia; empty lacunae), then **repair from the living margin**: hyperaemia, granulation tissue, **creeping substitution** (new bone laid on dead trabeculae, then resorption).
- **Collapse** occurs during **repair**, not at the moment of death: resorption at the junction of dead and living bone weakens the subchondral plate, producing a **subchondral fracture (crescent sign)** and then flattening of the head.
- Necrotic bone **looks normal on radiographs** for weeks to months (no change until repair produces sclerosis and resorption).

## 5. Clinical features
- **Groin pain** (sometimes buttock or knee), worse with weight bearing; rest and night pain in some; sudden worsening suggests **collapse**.
- **Painful, limited internal rotation**, antalgic gait; later loss of all movements.
- Early lesions are often **asymptomatic** (found in the contralateral hip or at screening of high-risk patients).

## 6. Investigations
### Plain radiographs (AP pelvis and **frog-leg lateral**)
- Normal early.
- Then **mottled sclerosis and cysts**.
- **Crescent sign:** subchondral radiolucent line = **subchondral fracture**; seen best on the **frog-leg lateral**; marks the start of collapse (poor prognosis for head preservation).
- Then **flattening/collapse**, and finally **joint-space narrowing** and acetabular changes (OA).

### MRI: investigation of choice
- **Most sensitive and specific** (about 99%) and the best test for **early (pre-radiographic) disease** and for screening the **contralateral hip**.
- **T1:** **single serpiginous low-signal band** (the reactive interface) outlining the necrotic segment, which often keeps fat signal.
- **T2:** **"double-line sign"**: an inner **high-signal** line (hyperaemic granulation tissue) beside an outer **low-signal** line (sclerotic bone). **Pathognomonic.**
- **Bone marrow oedema** with a known lesion suggests **imminent or recent collapse** and correlates with pain.
- MRI also measures **lesion size and location**, the main prognostic factors.

### Other tests
- **CT:** best to detect **subchondral fracture and early collapse** (more sensitive than radiographs); useful for planning.
- **Bone scan:** **"cold in hot"** (photopenic centre with surrounding increased uptake, "doughnut"); less sensitive than MRI; useful for multifocal screening when MRI is not possible.
- **Work-up for cause:** lipids, coagulation profile/thrombophilia screen where idiopathic or multifocal, haemoglobin electrophoresis, HIV, uric acid, glucose.
- **Multifocal osteonecrosis** (3 or more sites; about 3% of patients): almost always **steroid-related or coagulopathy**; screen other joints (knees, shoulders).

## 7. Classification
### Ficat and Arlet (modified): the classic exam system
| Stage | Radiograph | MRI | Clinical |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | Normal | Normal / abnormal (preclinical) | No symptoms |
| **I** | Normal | **Abnormal** | Pain possible |
| **II** | **Sclerosis, cysts**; normal head contour | Abnormal | Pain |
| **III** | **Crescent sign**, subchondral collapse, flattening | Abnormal | Pain, stiffness |
| **IV** | **Joint-space narrowing, acetabular changes (OA)** | Abnormal | Severe |

- The **transition from II to III (pre-collapse to collapse)** is the key management watershed: joint-preserving procedures work best **before collapse**.

### ARCO 2019 revised staging (Association Research Circulation Osseous)
| Stage | Findings |
|---|---|
| **I** | Radiograph **normal**, **MRI positive** (band-like lesion) |
| **II** | Radiograph **abnormal** (sclerosis, osteolysis, focal osteoporosis), **no collapse** |
| **IIIA (early)** | **Subchondral fracture or collapse of 2 mm or less** |
| **IIIB (late)** | **Collapse over 2 mm** |
| **IV** | **Osteoarthritis** (joint-space narrowing, acetabular changes) |

- ARCO 2019 **dropped stage 0** and the old subclassification by lesion size and location from the staging itself (these are assessed separately).

### Steinberg (University of Pennsylvania)
- Stages **0 to VI** (VI = advanced degeneration) with **quantification of lesion size**: **A (under 15% of the head), B (15-30%), C (over 30%)**; stage IV and V also graded by extent of surface collapse and acetabular involvement.

### Prognostic size and location systems
| System | How | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Japanese Investigation Committee (JIC) type** | Location of the necrotic area relative to the **weight-bearing portion** on the AP | **A** (medial third), **B** (medial two-thirds), **C1** (beyond two-thirds but within the acetabular edge), **C2** (extends **lateral to the acetabular edge**). **C1/C2 have a high collapse risk**; A rarely collapses |
| **Modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle** (Ha et al.) | **Sum of the arc of necrosis on mid-coronal and mid-sagittal MRI** | **Under 190 degrees: low risk** of collapse; **190-240: intermediate**; **240 or more: high risk** (grades I to IV: under 160, 160-199, 200-239, 240 or more) |

- **Natural history:** asymptomatic, **small (under 15%), medial (JIC A) lesions** often never collapse; **large (over 30%) or lateral (JIC C2) lesions** collapse in the majority (often over 50-80%) within a few years. **Once symptomatic, most untreated lesions progress.**

## 8. Management of osteonecrosis of the femoral head
### Determinants of treatment
- **Stage (pre-collapse vs collapse)**, **lesion size and location**, **symptoms**, **age and activity**, **cause** (ongoing steroid use, sickle cell), and **contralateral hip**.
- **Modify risk factors:** reduce steroids where possible, stop alcohol and smoking, treat coagulopathy.

### Non-operative and pharmacological options
- **Observation** with serial MRI for **small, asymptomatic, medial** lesions.
- **Protected weight bearing** alone does **not** alter natural history.
- **Bisphosphonates (alendronate, zoledronate):** aim to slow resorption of the necrotic segment and delay collapse. Indian (Agarwala) and some other series were favourable, but **RCTs (e.g. Chen et al. 2012) showed no benefit**: **debated**, not standard.
- **Statins** (reduce steroid-induced adipogenesis; observational), **anticoagulants** (enoxaparin in thrombophilia, small studies), **iloprost** (prostacyclin analogue for marrow oedema), **extracorporeal shock wave therapy**, **hyperbaric oxygen**, pulsed electromagnetic fields: adjuncts with limited evidence.

### Core decompression (CD)
- **Indication:** **symptomatic pre-collapse** lesions (**Ficat I-II / ARCO I-II**), best for **small to medium** lesions.
- **Rationale:** relieves raised intraosseous pressure, removes necrotic bone, stimulates repair; also gives a biopsy.
- **Technique:**
  1. Lateral incision; under fluoroscopy, guide wire from the lateral cortex **at or above the level of the lesser trochanter** (an entry **below the lesser trochanter** creates a stress riser and **subtrochanteric fracture**, the main complication).
  2. Advance into the necrotic lesion to within about **3-5 mm of the subchondral plate** without breaching it (penetration of the articular surface is a pitfall).
  3. Classic single **8-10 mm trephine core**, or **multiple small-diameter drillings (about 3 mm; Mont)** which reduce fracture risk.
  4. **Protected weight bearing** for about 6 weeks.
- **Augmentation:** **bone marrow aspirate concentrate / autologous mesenchymal cells** (Hernigou; **Gangji** and other RCTs) improves outcome in pre-collapse lesions; also bone graft, synthetic substitutes, porous tantalum rods (high failure, abandoned), BMP.
- **Results:** best for **Ficat I** and small lesions; **poor once collapse has occurred** (crescent sign).

### Bone grafting procedures
- **Non-vascularised:**
  - **Phemister** (cortical strut through a core track).
  - **"Lightbulb" / trapdoor** techniques: window at the head-neck junction (lightbulb) or through the articular cartilage (trapdoor), debride necrotic bone and pack graft.
- **Vascularised fibular graft (Urbaniak, Duke):** for **young patients**, pre-collapse and **early collapse** (ARCO IIIA) with medium-large lesions; good head survival in experienced hands; donor site morbidity (ankle pain, weakness of great toe flexion, peroneal nerve).
- **Muscle-pedicle bone grafts:** **quadratus femoris** pedicle (**Meyers**, posterior), tensor fascia lata, iliacus/sartorius; **Baksi** popularised muscle-pedicle grafting in India.

### Osteotomies
- **Principle:** **move the necrotic segment out of the weight-bearing zone** and bring healthy cartilage under load.
- **Sugioka transtrochanteric anterior rotational osteotomy:** rotates the head about the neck axis so the anterior necrotic segment moves anteriorly/inferiorly; popular in **Japan**; needs intact posterior head (healthy area **over a third** of the weight-bearing surface); risk of further AVN of the head and non-union.
- **Intertrochanteric varus or valgus (flexion/extension) osteotomies:** for lesions with a **combined necrotic angle under about 200 degrees**; may make later THA harder.

### Arthroplasty
- **Total hip arthroplasty:** treatment of choice for **collapse with symptoms** in most adults (**ARCO IIIB-IV, Ficat III-IV**) and large lesions where preservation is unlikely; modern **cementless** THA results in ONFH are **now similar to OA**, though young age, high activity and some aetiologies raise revision risk.
  - **Sickle cell disease:** higher rates of **infection, bleeding, sickling crises, revision**; preoperative transfusion, hydration, warmth, oxygenation; hard sclerotic bone (canal obliteration) can cause **femoral perforation/fracture**.
  - **Renal transplant / steroid users:** infection risk, poor bone.
  - **Gaucher:** bleeding (thrombocytopenia).
- **Hemiarthroplasty (bipolar)** and **hemiresurfacing:** **not recommended** routinely (persistent groin pain, acetabular erosion); hemiresurfacing is reserved for selected young patients with intact acetabular cartilage.
- **Hip resurfacing:** limited by a large necrotic segment (inadequate bone for the component) and metal-on-metal concerns.

### Summary algorithm (generally accepted)
| Situation | Preferred option |
|---|---|
| Asymptomatic, small/medial lesion (under 15%, JIC A, necrotic angle under 190) | **Observe**, serial MRI, risk-factor modification |
| Asymptomatic, large or lateral lesion | Consider **core decompression** (debated) |
| **Symptomatic pre-collapse** (Ficat I-II / ARCO I-II), small-medium | **Core decompression ± cell therapy / bone graft** |
| Pre-collapse or early collapse (ARCO IIIA), large lesion, young | **Vascularised fibular graft**, bone grafting, or **rotational osteotomy** |
| **Collapse over 2 mm (ARCO IIIB), or OA (IV)**, symptomatic | **Total hip arthroplasty** |

> Exam pearl: **Steroids** = commonest non-traumatic cause (over **2 g prednisolone in 3 months**, ARCO). **MRI** = investigation of choice (**double-line sign on T2**). **Crescent sign** = subchondral fracture, best on the **frog-leg lateral**, start of collapse. **Core decompression** only works **before collapse**; enter **above the lesser trochanter**. Collapsed symptomatic head in an adult = **THA**. Always MRI the **other hip**.

## 9. Differential diagnosis: transient osteoporosis of the hip (bone marrow oedema syndrome)
| Feature | **Transient osteoporosis** | **Osteonecrosis** |
|---|---|---|
| Patient | **Third-trimester pregnancy (often left hip)**, middle-aged men | 30-50 years, risk factors |
| MRI | **Diffuse marrow oedema** of head **and neck** extending to intertrochanteric region, **no focal subchondral band / double line** | **Focal, well-demarcated band**, double line on T2 |
| Radiograph | **Regional osteopenia** after weeks | Sclerosis, crescent, collapse |
| Course | **Self-limiting over 6-12 months**; may migrate (regional migratory osteoporosis) | Often progressive |
| Treatment | **Protected weight bearing** (risk of **femoral neck fracture**), analgesia; bisphosphonates may shorten course | Stage-based |

- **Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the femoral head:** elderly osteoporotic women or after transplant; low-signal subchondral line **convex to the articular surface** (an osteonecrosis band is **concave** to it) with surrounding oedema; may collapse rapidly (rapidly destructive coxopathy).

## 10. Osteonecrosis at other sites
### Knee
| Feature | **SONK / SIFK (spontaneous)** | **Secondary osteonecrosis** | **Post-arthroscopic** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Patient | **Women over 55-60** | **Under 45**, steroids, alcohol, SLE, sickle cell | After meniscectomy/chondroplasty |
| Onset | **Sudden severe medial knee pain**, night pain | Gradual | Weeks after arthroscopy |
| Site | **Single, epiphyseal, medial femoral condyle** (weight-bearing) | **Multiple lesions**, often **bilateral** (over 80%), **epiphysis and metaphysis/diaphysis**, other joints involved | Usually medial femoral condyle |
| Pathology | Now recognised as a **subchondral insufficiency fracture (SIFK)**, often with a **medial meniscus posterior root tear** | True ischaemic necrosis | |

- **Prognosis (SONK):** small lesions (**under about 3.5 cm squared, or less than about 40% of condylar width** on AP) often settle with **protected weight bearing and analgesia**; large lesions progress to collapse and need **UKA/TKA** (or HTO with grafting in younger patients). Staging by Koshino/Aglietti.
- **Secondary osteonecrosis:** core decompression/drilling for pre-collapse lesions; **TKA** after collapse (stemmed components may be needed if metaphyseal involvement).

### Humeral head
- **Second commonest site of non-traumatic osteonecrosis** (steroids, sickle cell, dysbaric) and after 4-part fractures.
- **Cruess staging** (I normal radiograph/MRI positive; II sclerosis; III crescent sign; IV collapse; V glenoid involvement).
- Better tolerated than the hip (non-weight-bearing). Core decompression early; **hemiarthroplasty or resurfacing** for collapse with intact glenoid; **TSA** when the glenoid is involved.

### Talus
- After **talar neck fractures** (Hawkins classification: AVN risk rises from type I to IV, up to about 100% in type IV in older series).
- **Hawkins sign:** **subchondral lucency of the talar dome at 6-8 weeks** on AP ankle radiograph = **intact blood supply** (bone resorption from disuse needs vascularity); its **absence suggests** (does not prove) AVN.
- Revascularisation occurs by creeping substitution over many months; weight bearing need not be delayed until full revascularisation (debated). Collapse: ankle/tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis (Blair fusion historically) or talar replacement.

### Wrist and other eponymous osteonecroses / osteochondroses
| Eponym | Site | Typical patient |
|---|---|---|
| **Perthes** | Femoral head | Boys 4-8 years |
| **Kienbock** | **Lunate** | Young adult men; **negative ulnar variance**; Lichtman staging |
| **Preiser** | **Scaphoid** (idiopathic, non-traumatic) | Adults |
| Scaphoid proximal pole after fracture | Scaphoid | Retrograde blood supply from distal pole (dorsal ridge vessels of radial artery) |
| **Freiberg** | **Second metatarsal head** (commonest) | **Adolescent girls**, long second metatarsal |
| **Kohler** | **Tarsal navicular** | Boys 4-6 years; self-limiting, cast if painful |
| **Panner** | **Capitellum** | Boys **under 10**; self-limiting (vs OCD of capitellum in adolescent throwers/gymnasts) |
| **Sever** | Calcaneal apophysis | Apophysitis (not true osteonecrosis), 8-12 years |
| **Osgood-Schlatter / Sinding-Larsen-Johansson** | Tibial tubercle / inferior patellar pole | Traction apophysitis |
| **Scheuermann** | Thoracic vertebral endplates | Adolescents; 3 or more adjacent vertebrae wedged 5 degrees or more |
| **Calve** | Vertebral body (vertebra plana) | Usually **eosinophilic granuloma** (Langerhans cell histiocytosis), not osteonecrosis |
| **Kummell disease** | Vertebral body | Delayed post-traumatic collapse with **intravertebral vacuum cleft** |

### Sickle cell disease: orthopaedic summary
- **Femoral head AVN** (common, often bilateral, early adulthood), humeral head AVN, **dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome)** in infants, **H-shaped ("Lincoln log") vertebrae**, bone infarcts.
- **Osteomyelitis: Salmonella** is classically characteristic, but **Staphylococcus aureus remains common** (and is the commonest in many series); **distinguishing infarction from infection** is difficult (both cause pain, fever, raised markers): MRI, ultrasound-guided aspiration, blood cultures.

> Exam pearl: **Hawkins sign present = good** (vascularity intact). **SONK** = elderly woman, sudden pain, **single medial femoral condyle** lesion (really a subchondral insufficiency fracture); **secondary knee osteonecrosis** = young, steroids, **multiple and bilateral**. **Transient osteoporosis** = diffuse oedema without a double line, third trimester, self-limiting.
